messages.author: f1a78b77bed56547
messages.subject: remove reactivity
parts:
Hi,

I'm using uiOutput and renderUI to dynamically create a Shiny app. As the app itself fluctuates, how may I remove a previously established reactive dependency?

In ?observe I found the "destroy()" method, but I'm not sure how to use it, and it does not appear to apply to reactive().

Jonathan

messages.author: ca443e6eaa0e78ed
messages.subject: Re: remove reactivity
parts:
You generally don't need to do this, especially for reactive(). Reactive expressions are lazily executed, so if you stop calling it, it never executes.

If you could provide a minimal example of what you're talking about, that would be really helpful, thanks.

Jonathan

messages.subject: Re: remove reactivity
parts:
The app starts with a simple  interface, that just asks for a text input file. The app then adds more buttons and sliders and outputs on the fly based on the file contents. At that point the user may pick a different file, and everything would 'regenerate' based on the contents of the file. This seems straight forward using uiOutput and renderUI.  Except that all these dangling observer() and reactive() calls are registering a reactive response somewhere, and it seems could quickly cause problems.

Actually, that's another challenge. In the regenerated case, can or how may I call observer() and reactive() from within a "renderUI"? Maybe what I describe is simply not possible. Is there some kind of work around, like two apps that talk to each other somehow? Perhaps through a query string? But that would seem very very slow responding compared with using renderUI on the fly.

Jonathan

messages.subject: Re: remove reactivity
parts:
I have a similar issue, I call destroy() on my newly created observers, but it doesn't seem to work, they stay alive 
Is this a bug?

Thanks
Jacques

---------server.R ----------------
# Create some observer dynamically from test.R
withReactiveDomain(session, eval(parse(text="source('test.R',local=TRUE) ")) )

--------- test.R ------------------
if(is.null(observerpool$test)) {
  observerpool$test <<- observe({
        #reactive code etc.
       input$xxx
       ....
       ....
  })
}

--------------server.R -------------------------
# Try to destroy all dynamic observers at a later stage...
isolate({
      obsinst = names(observerpool);
      lapply(obsinst,function(t) {
        obs = eval(parse(text=paste("observerpool$",as.character(t) ,sep="") ))
        if(!is.null(obs)) {
          print(paste("DESTROY() ", as.character(t),sep=""))
          obs$destroy();
          print("Done")
        } else {
          print("Observer is NULL")
        }
        eval(parse(text=paste("observerpool$",as.character(t)," <<- NULL;" ,sep="") ))
      })
    });  
----------------------------------------------------------

messages.author: ca443e6eaa0e78ed
messages.subject: Re: remove reactivity
parts:
I don't suppose your app is on GitHub? I'd be very interested in seeing what you're doing.

It sounds to me like maybe you're expecting:

obs <- observe({
  r1 <- reactive(...)
  r2 <- reactive(...)
  output$plot <- renderPlot(... r1() ... r2() ...)
})
obs$destroy()

that the destroy() call would halt the plot and reactive inside. That's not the case.

The main thing I would say is that generally, it's not even close to being worth the effort to "destroy" outputs, reactives, etc. These things take zero computational overhead when they're not executing (though they do hold on to memory if they can't be garbage collected). Shiny assumes that outputs that aren't visible on the page shouldn't be executed and will automatically suspend them. Unless you're actually seeing these outputs unnecessarily executing, or the memory pressure is particularly high, I wouldn't worry about it.

Yesterday I merged a new Shiny Modules feature that you may be interested in. http://shiny.rstudio.com/articles/modules.html It should simplify the creation of your components. There's nothing that it does to help with destroying modules, but as I noted above I assume that that's not often needed.
